Principal
prĭn´sĭ-păl
adj. and n. (chief; first in rank; also, the original sum owed; Hebrew rosh, re'shith)
Latin principalis, first, chief, from princeps. In the KJV it carries both senses English still has: what ranks first, and the original capital of a debt.

Biblical Definition

Principal serves two senses in the KJV, and both are exact. It marks the chief or best of a kind: “Take thou also unto thee principal spices, of pure myrrh five hundred shekels, and of sweet cinnamon half so much” (Exo 30:23), the ingredients of the holy anointing oil. It marks rank: “And Azariah the son of Nathan was over the officers: and Zabud the son of Nathan was principal officer, and the king's friend” (1Ki 4:5), and “the principal scribe of the host, which mustered the people of the land” (2Ki 25:19), taken by the Babylonians at the fall of Jerusalem. And it carries the financial sense in the law of restitution: “Then they shall confess their sin which they have done: and he shall recompense his trespass with the principal thereof, and add unto it the fifth part thereof, and give it unto him against whom he hath trespassed” (Num 5:7). Above all it names what a man should want most: “Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding” (Pro 4:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines principal as chief; highest in rank, character or importance; and, as a noun, a capital sum lent on interest, or the original sum of a debt.

expand to see more

PRINCIPAL, a. Chief; highest in rank, character or respectability.

2. Chief; most important or considerable; as the principal reason.

PRINCIPAL, n. A chief or head; one who takes the lead.

2. A capital sum lent on interest, due as a debt or used as a fund; so called as being the head or chief, distinguished from interest or profits.

Key Scripture

Exo 30:23 — "Take thou also unto thee principal spices, of pure myrrh five hundred shekels, and of sweet cinnamon half so much, even two hundred and fifty shekels, and of sweet calamus two hundred and fifty shekels,"

Num 5:7 — "Then they shall confess their sin which they have done: and he shall recompense his trespass with the principal thereof, and add unto it the fifth part thereof, and give it unto him against whom he hath trespassed."

1Ki 4:5 — "And Azariah the son of Nathan was over the officers: and Zabud the son of Nathan was principal officer, and the king's friend:"

Pro 4:7 — "Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding."

Modern Corruption

Repentance is treated as a matter of feeling and apology, while Numbers 5 requires the principal restored and a fifth added on top.

expand to see more

Numbers 5:7 is one of the most practical verses on repentance in Scripture and one of the least preached. Confession comes first — they shall confess their sin which they have done — and then the principal is restored, and a fifth part added, to the person actually wronged. Not to the temple, not to a general fund, and not in place of the confession. Zacchaeus understood the law and went well past it, and the Lord Jesus called that day salvation come to his house.

The other sense governs Proverbs 4:7, which is the Bible's clearest statement of priority: Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding. The verse assumes a man will be getting things — it does not scold him for it — and it fixes what must be got first. Solomon, who wrote it, asked for exactly that and was given the rest besides, which is the pattern the Lord repeats in Matthew 6: seek ye first the kingdom of God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rosh (H7218), head, chief — both the principal spices and the principal of a debt; re'shith (H7225), beginning, first; chomesh (H2549), the fifth part added in restitution.

expand to see more

Hebrew rosh (H7218) — head, chief, principal; Exodus 30:23, Numbers 5:7.

Hebrew re'shith (H7225) — beginning, chief; Proverbs 4:7, wisdom is the principal thing.

Hebrew chomesh (H2549) — a fifth part; added to the principal in restitution.

Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom; the principal thing to be got.

Hebrew 'asham (H817) — trespass, guilt offering; the setting of the restitution law.

Usage

"“Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom” — first, not only."

"“He shall recompense his trespass with the principal thereof, and add unto it the fifth part” — repentance with a ledger."

"“Take thou also unto thee principal spices” — the best of the kind, for the holy oil."
